chapters.title: Same room, or a phone call

scenes.narration: Your server works on your laptop. Putting it on the internet takes one word.

It also takes two settings that quietly switch features off if you don't know what they do — and you'll leave knowing exactly which features, and where those settings actually live. Learn MCP, on THE NBX STUDIO.

There are two transports worth knowing, and they carry exactly the same JSON. Stdio means the client launches the server as a child process on the same machine and they talk over standard input and standard output — like two people at one desk passing notes. Every feature works, setup is nothing, and it only ever works locally. Streamable H T T P means the server runs somewhere else entirely and you reach it over the network, which is what you need the moment the server isn't on the user's laptop. That's the whole choice: stdio while you're developing, H T T P when you ship.

mcpTransport.caption: two transports
mcpTransport.premise: Both move identical JSON. The only difference is whether the two programs share a machine.

scenes.narration: Stdio deserves a closer look, because how it works explains a bug almost everyone hits once. The client doesn't connect to a running server. The client LAUNCHES the server as a child process, and then talks to it down that process's own standard input and standard output. So standard out isn't where your program prints — it is the wire. Which means a stray print, left in from debugging, writes a line of plain text into the middle of a JSON-RPC stream, and the client fails to parse it. The error you get points at JSON, not at the print statement that caused it, which is why this one costs people an afternoon. Print to standard error instead — the client leaves that alone, and you'll see it in your terminal. And now the logging deprecation from the last chapter makes sense: standard error is exactly where the spec is telling you to send logs.

scenes.narration: Now the trap, and it's worth reading twice. First, where these flags actually live, because this catches anyone who learnt MCP a year ago: they are not constructor arguments. You pass them to run, alongside the transport, and the server object itself knows nothing about them. Stateless h t t p true means the server forgets each client between requests, which is exactly what you want behind a load balancer, because any instance can then answer any request. The cost is severe, though: sampling stops working, elicitation stops working, roots stop working, and subscriptions stop working — every one of those needs the server to remember who you are between calls. Json response true means replies come back as plain JSON instead of a stream, which kills live progress and log messages, since streaming is the mechanism those travel on. Notice what survives both: ordinary tool calls. So start with both false, which is the default, and only reach for either when you genuinely need horizontal scaling and can say out loud what you're giving up.

scenes.narration: Three lines. Stdio is for development, on one machine. Streamable H T T P is for production, across the network. And both flags default to false for a reason — turning either on trades features for scale.
